We use the combined LCAO and VB method introduced in Section 6.12, in which the s framework is constructed by overlap of C and O sp2 hybrid orbitals and H 1s orbitals using the VB approach and the p bonds are constructed using the LCAO MO method. We follow the procedures developed in Section 6.5 and label the orbitals using the same notation that we use for diatomic molecules, even though these molecules are not cylindrically symmetric; we have s, s*, p, p*, and n (nonbonding) orbitals to use in our discussion. The nonbonding orbitals are occupied by lone pairs on heteroatoms such as oxygen, nitrogen, and sulfur, which play important roles in spectroscopy and photochemistry.

The Lewis dot model for ethylene shows that it has 12 valence electrons, 8 of which are in the four localized CUH s orbitals, the remaining four being associ- ated with the CuC bond. The CUH s orbitals lie too low in energy to play any significant role in the spectroscopy and photochemistry of ethylene so we consider only those MOs associated with the CuC bond. These include the s and s* and the p and p* orbitals that are derived from the carbon 2pz and 2px (or 2py) orbit- als, respectively, as shown in Figure 20.29. The energy level separation (splitting) between the s and s* orbitals is greater than that between the p and p* orbitals because “end-to-end” overlap of the pz orbitals to form s bonds is greater than the “side-to-side” overlap of the px (or py) orbitals that form p bonds, as discussed in Section 6.5. The lowest energy configuration is (s)2(p)2, in the notation used by spectroscopists and photochemists, a shorthand version of the notation we intro- duced in Section 6.5. Ethylene has a double bond, with two electrons occupying each of the two bonding MOs. The highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) is the bonding p orbital, and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) is the anti- bonding p* orbital. These frontier orbitals are of central importance in spectros- copy, photochemistry, and in many organic chemical reaction mechanisms because changes in the occupancy of these orbitals affect bond order and reactivity.
